words.definition: To make someone feel hostile or indifferent toward people they were once close to.
words.example: After years of bitter arguments over money, he became estranged from his brother and they stopped speaking entirely.
words.mnemonic: e-STRANGE: you start treating a once-close person like a total STRANGER.

words.definition: Having a similar character, background, or set of feelings to another.
words.example: They turned out to be kindred spirits, loving the same obscure films and finishing each other's sentences.
words.mnemonic: KIN + dred: your KIN are your family — people who are alike and connected to you.

words.definition: A small area or group that differs culturally from the larger territory surrounding it.
words.example: The old fishing village survived as a quiet Portuguese enclave in the middle of the sprawling modern city.
words.mnemonic: en-CLAVE sounds like 'in a cave' — a sealed pocket tucked inside something much bigger.

words.definition: The scattering of a people away from their original homeland across many countries.
words.example: The famine drove millions abroad, creating an Irish diaspora that reached nearly every continent.
words.mnemonic: DIA (across) + SPORA (seeds): seeds scattered across the earth, like spores blown far from the plant.

words.definition: A person residing in a country other than the one where they were born.
words.example: As an expatriate in Tokyo, she gathered with other Americans each November to cook Thanksgiving dinner far from home.
words.mnemonic: ex- (out of) + patria (fatherland): someone living OUT of their FATHERLAND.

words.definition: Originating and living naturally in a particular region rather than arriving from elsewhere.
words.example: Kangaroos are indigenous to Australia and are found in the wild nowhere else on Earth.
words.mnemonic: Root 'gen' means born; 'indi' hints at inside — born inside this very land, an 'indie' original of the place.

words.definition: To grant full legal citizenship to someone born in another country.
words.example: After living in Canada for six years, he was naturalized and proudly voted in his first election.
words.mnemonic: Make a newcomer a NATURAL: treat them as if they naturally belonged as a citizen all along.

words.definition: A small, exclusive circle of people sharing common interests or tastes.
words.example: The aging poet dined each night with his coterie of loyal admirers and fellow writers.
words.mnemonic: COTERIE sounds like 'CATER-ie' — the tight inner group everyone rushes to CATER to.

words.definition: A tight, exclusive group that keeps outsiders from joining.
words.example: In high school the popular clique claimed the same lunch table and ignored anyone who tried to sit down.
words.mnemonic: CLIQUE sounds like 'CLICK' — the in-group that 'clicks' together and locks everyone else out.

words.definition: The physical or social setting in which a person lives or something takes place.
words.example: Raised in an academic milieu, she grew up surrounded by crowded bookshelves and lively dinner-table debate.
words.mnemonic: French mi-lieu = 'middle place': the surroundings you stand in the MIDDLE of.

words.definition: Narrow-minded and cut off from outside people, cultures, or ideas.
words.example: The remote mountain town was so insular that any stranger was met with years of lasting suspicion.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'insula' means ISLAND — an island mind, walled off from the mainland by water.

words.definition: Familiar with and comfortable among many different countries and cultures.
words.example: London felt wonderfully cosmopolitan, offering cuisines, languages, and festivals from every corner of the globe.
words.mnemonic: COSMO (world) + POLITAN (citizen): a citizen of the whole COSMOS — at home anywhere on Earth.

words.definition: Limited in outlook and unsophisticated, typical of places far from a big city.
words.example: His provincial tastes were obvious the moment he refused any dish he couldn't already pronounce.
words.mnemonic: Think PROVINCE — someone stuck out in a distant province, far from the wider, worldlier city.

words.definition: Intense dislike or fear of people from other countries.
words.example: Rising xenophobia led the angry crowd to blame recent immigrants for every problem the town faced.
words.mnemonic: XENO (stranger) + PHOBIA (fear): a fear of anything strange or foreign.

words.definition: A policy of protecting the interests of established inhabitants against those of immigrants.
words.example: The party's nativism promised local jobs to locals first and sharply restricted all new arrivals.
words.mnemonic: NATIVE + ism: the belief that the native-born should always come first.

words.definition: The recorded line of ancestors from which a person or animal descends.
words.example: The breeder produced a pedigree tracing the puppy's champion bloodline back six generations.
words.mnemonic: From French 'pied de grue' (foot of a crane) — the branching lines of a family chart look like a crane's splayed foot.

words.definition: The image or character someone presents to others, often masking their true self.
words.example: Offstage he was shy, but his brash rock-star persona commanded every arena.
words.mnemonic: In Latin theatre a 'persona' was the mask an actor held up — a face worn over the real one.

words.definition: The quality of being genuine, real, and true to its origin.
words.example: Experts tested the pigment and canvas to confirm the painting's authenticity before the auction.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'author' inside it — something authentic can be traced to its real author or source.

words.definition: A person who comes from the same country as another.
words.example: Stranded at the foreign airport, she was thrilled to meet a compatriot who spoke her language.
words.mnemonic: 'com-' (together) + 'patriot' — patriots who share the same fatherland.

words.definition: A person, animal, or plant that lives in a particular place.
words.example: Owls and other nocturnal denizens of the forest emerged only after sunset.
words.mnemonic: 'den' + 'izen' — the creature curled up in its den is that den's denizen.

words.definition: Traveling from place to place, especially to find work.
words.example: The itinerant preacher never stayed in one town for more than a week.
words.mnemonic: Share the root of 'itinerary' (Latin 'iter', journey) — always on the next leg of a journey.

words.definition: Roaming from place to place rather than living in one fixed home.
words.example: The nomadic herders followed the rains, packing their tents whenever the grass ran out.
words.mnemonic: 'No-mad' — a nomad is in no mad rush to settle down; they wander at will.

words.definition: Forced to leave one's home or normal position.
words.example: The flood left thousands of displaced families sheltering in school gymnasiums.
words.mnemonic: 'dis-' (away) + 'placed' — taken away from your place.

words.definition: A safe place offering shelter, or a sacred area within a temple.
words.example: Fleeing the storm, the hikers found sanctuary in an old stone chapel.
words.mnemonic: Root 'sanct-' means holy (as in 'sacred') — a sanctuary is protected, untouchable ground.

words.definition: Protection granted by a country to someone fleeing danger elsewhere.
words.example: The journalist applied for asylum after being threatened for exposing the regime.
words.mnemonic: Greek 'a-' (without) + 'sylon' (right of seizure) — a place where you cannot be seized.

words.definition: Faithfulness and loyalty to a person, cause, or duty.
words.example: Her fidelity to the company never wavered, even through years of layoffs.
words.mnemonic: Think of the dog named Fido — from Latin 'fides' (faith), the very picture of loyalty.

words.definition: To combine or unite separate things into a single whole.
words.example: The two rival banks decided to amalgamate into one national institution.
words.mnemonic: Picture a dental 'amalgam' — a filling that fuses several metals into one solid mass.

words.definition: An original model or perfect example on which others are based.
words.example: Sherlock Holmes became the archetype for nearly every brilliant fictional detective after him.
words.mnemonic: 'arch-' (chief/first, as in 'archangel') + 'type' — the first, master type others copy.

words.definition: A fixed, oversimplified belief about all members of a group.
words.example: The comedian's whole act relied on a tired stereotype about clumsy tourists.
words.mnemonic: Greek 'stereo-' (solid/rigid, as in a printing plate) + 'type' — one hard template stamped onto everyone.

words.definition: The everyday language spoken by ordinary people of a particular region.
words.example: Instead of formal Latin, the poet wrote in the local vernacular so farmers could read him.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'verna' meant a home-born servant — hence the plain, home-grown speech of a place.

words.definition: Strong loyalty to one's own group, often paired with hostility toward outsiders.
words.example: Once the debate began, tribalism took over and each side cheered only for its own team.
words.mnemonic: 'Tribe' + '-ism' — the belief that your tribe comes first, everyone else second.

words.definition: To mix and socialize in a friendly way, often with people one shouldn't.
words.example: The sergeant warned the new recruits not to fraternize with soldiers from the enemy camp.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'frater' (brother) — to treat someone like a brother, buddy up.

words.definition: A person whom everyone rejects and refuses to associate with.
words.example: After the scandal broke, the once-popular banker became a pariah nobody would sit beside.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'pa-RYE-ah' — imagine someone left alone to eat dry rye bread while everyone else avoids them.

words.definition: Someone driven out of a group and no longer accepted by it.
words.example: The new student ate lunch alone every day, treated like an outcast by the older kids.
words.mnemonic: 'Out' + 'cast' — someone who has been cast out of the group.

words.definition: The state of being forced to live away from one's own country.
words.example: The deposed king spent the rest of his life in exile, never allowed to return home.
words.mnemonic: 'Ex-' (out of) + 'isle' — pushed out and stranded on a distant island, far from home.

words.definition: A person who flees their homeland to escape war, disaster, or persecution.
words.example: The family became refugees overnight, packing one bag before crossing the border to safety.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'refuge' — someone seeking refuge, a safe place away from danger.

words.definition: A person who intrudes into a place or affair where they do not belong.
words.example: The regulars at the tavern eyed the stranger like an interloper who had wandered into their private club.
words.mnemonic: 'Inter-' (between) + 'lope' — someone who lopes in between where they weren't invited.

words.definition: To gradually get used to a new environment or set of conditions.
words.example: It took the mountaineers a week to acclimate to the thin air before the final climb.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'climate' — to adjust yourself to a new climate.

words.definition: The belief that personal independence and self-reliance matter more than group needs.
words.example: Raised on rugged individualism, she preferred solving her own problems to asking anyone for help.
words.mnemonic: Built on 'individual' — putting the single person, the individual, above the crowd.

words.definition: Deserving blame for having done something wrong.
words.example: The report found the manager culpable for ignoring the safety warnings that led to the fire.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'culpa' (fault) — think 'mea culpa,' my fault; a culpable person is at fault.

words.definition: Involved with others in a wrongful or illegal act.
words.example: By staying silent about the cheating, the whole class became complicit in it.
words.mnemonic: Related to 'accomplice' — a complicit person acts like a quiet accomplice.

words.definition: Kept hidden and carried out in secret, usually because it is not allowed.
words.example: The rebels held clandestine meetings in a cellar so the soldiers would never find them.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'clan' + 'destine' — a clan destined to meet in the shadows, hidden away.

words.definition: Done quietly and by stealth to avoid being noticed.
words.example: He took a surreptitious glance at his phone under the desk while the teacher wrote on the board.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'sir-REP-titious' — imagine a sneaky 'serpent' slipping in unseen.

words.definition: Behaving in a secretive, sneaky way that suggests something is being hidden.
words.example: Her furtive glances toward the door made everyone suspect she was about to slip away.
words.mnemonic: Shares roots with 'fur' in 'furtive' — think of a cat-burglar in a fur coat, moving in shady silence.

words.definition: Felt or experienced through the actions and feelings of another person.
words.example: Watching her son score the winning goal gave her a vicarious thrill, as if she had played herself.
words.mnemonic: Related to 'vicar,' a stand-in for a higher authority — you feel it through a stand-in, not firsthand.

words.definition: Comfort or consolation given to someone after a loss or disappointment.
words.example: After the funeral, she found solace in long walks along the quiet shore.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'so less' — real comfort makes your grief feel so much less.

words.definition: Deprived of something or someone, and left empty as a result.
words.example: Bereft of her lifelong companion, she wandered the silent house for weeks.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'be left' — you are left with nothing.

words.definition: Cheerful, sociable, and fond of good company and celebration.
words.example: The convivial host kept everyone laughing and refilling their glasses all night.
words.mnemonic: con + VIVI (life, as in 'vivacious') — a gathering that is full of life.

words.definition: Excessively eager to obey or please others in a submissive, groveling way.
words.example: The waiter's servile bowing and scraping made the guests uncomfortable.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'servant' — behaving like a fawning, lowly servant.

words.definition: A person who flatters powerful people to gain advantage for themselves.
words.example: Surrounded by sycophants, the CEO never once heard an honest opinion.
words.mnemonic: Say 'SICK-o-fant' — a sickly flatterer who fawns to get ahead.

words.definition: Excessively smooth, oily, and insincere in manner or speech.
words.example: The salesman's unctuous compliments made her distrust him instantly.
words.mnemonic: From 'unction' (anointing oil) — think slippery, greasy charm.

words.definition: Preferring to live alone and avoid other people or society.
words.example: The reclusive author had not been photographed in over twenty years.
words.mnemonic: Think 'closed' off, like a monk shut away in a cloister.

words.definition: No longer content with or loyal to an authority or organization.
words.example: Disaffected voters stayed home rather than support either candidate.
words.mnemonic: dis- (not) + affection — you have lost the affection you once felt.

words.definition: Rigidly loyal to one group or faction, often causing bitter division.
words.example: Decades of sectarian conflict had split the city along religious lines.
words.mnemonic: SECT + -arian — someone fiercely devoted to their own narrow sect.

words.definition: To abandon or give up someone or something completely.
words.example: He promised never to forsake his friends, no matter how rich he became.
words.mnemonic: for + SAKE — you drop someone 'for the sake' of something else.

words.definition: Open to and welcoming of everyone, leaving no one out.
words.example: The club rewrote its rules to be more inclusive of newcomers.
words.mnemonic: in + -clude (to shut) — everyone is shut IN, nobody left outside.

words.definition: Pleasant and agreeable, especially because of a similar temperament.
words.example: The two strangers found each other congenial company and talked for hours.
words.mnemonic: con (with) + genial (friendly) — friendly and well-matched together.

words.definition: To reject someone or something with scorn or contempt.
words.example: She spurned his apology and walked away without a single word.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'spur' — you kick it away with your boot spur.

words.definition: To deliberately avoid or keep away from someone or something.
words.example: After the scandal broke, the whole town began to shun him.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'shoo' — you shoo away whatever you want to avoid.

words.definition: To be drawn steadily toward a particular person, place, or thing.
words.example: At parties he always gravitates toward the quietest corner of the room.
words.mnemonic: Root is 'gravity' — you are pulled toward it as if by an unseen force.

words.definition: Regularly traveling between different regions, usually depending on the changing seasons.
words.example: The lake fills with migratory geese every autumn, then falls silent once they head south.
words.mnemonic: Latin root migr- means 'to move'; picture a migr-atory flock moving across the sky each season.

words.definition: To permanently leave your own country in order to live somewhere else.
words.example: Facing no work at home, her grandparents chose to emigrate and start over across the ocean.
words.mnemonic: E = Exit: to Emigrate is to Exit your homeland (while immigrate means moving in).

words.definition: A person's usual mood and the natural way they tend to feel and react.
words.example: The puppy had such a gentle temperament that even nervous toddlers relaxed around it.
words.mnemonic: 'Temper' hides inside it — your everyday temper is a window into your whole temperament.

words.definition: The inherent qualities of mind and character that shape how someone typically behaves.
words.example: His sunny disposition meant he greeted even the rainiest Monday with a grin.
words.mnemonic: Dis-POSITION: think of how your character is 'positioned' by default before anything happens.

words.definition: Enduring pain or hardship calmly, without complaining or showing any feeling.
words.example: Even as the doctor set the broken bone, the old sailor stayed stoic and barely blinked.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'stone-ic' — stone-faced and unmoved no matter what hits you.

words.definition: Having no settled home or lasting ties to any place or community.
words.example: After a decade of drifting from city to city, she felt rootless and longed to finally belong somewhere.
words.mnemonic: Root + less: a plant with no roots drifts loose, just like a person with nowhere to hold on.
